title: Surgical Robotics and Navigation
answer: Resection planning, haptic feedback, virtual rehearsal, tremor stabilisation and telesurgery.

children.name: Resection Planning and Margins
children.blurb: Resection planning and margins concerns the preoperative and intraoperative determination of tissue to remove in cancer or other surgery, with the aim of achieving negative margins while preserving healthy function.

children.name: Haptic Feedback in Robotic Surgery
children.blurb: Haptic feedback in robotic surgery covers the sensing, transmission, and display of force, vibration, and texture information between surgical instruments and the surgeon's hands.

children.name: Virtual Surgical Rehearsal
children.blurb: Virtual surgical rehearsal uses patient-specific digital models to let a surgical team practice a planned procedure before entering the operating room.

children.name: Tremor Stabilisation in Microsurgery
children.blurb: Tremor stabilisation in microsurgery refers to technologies that reduce or cancel involuntary hand tremor during delicate procedures such as ophthalmology, neurosurgery, and vascular anastomosis.

children.name: Remote Telesurgery
children.blurb: Remote telesurgery is the practice of performing surgical procedures on a patient from a distant location using robotic instruments, a high-speed network, and real-time video and haptic feedback.

sections.body: Surgical robotics and navigation is the use of AI to help surgeons plan cuts, feel tissue through instruments, practice operations, steady their hands, and operate from a distance. In practice, AI now reads scans to suggest where a tumor ends and healthy tissue begins, which feeds into resection planning. Robotic systems use sensors and algorithms to give haptic feedback, so a surgeon feels resistance or texture through a controller. Virtual rehearsal lets a team run through a specific patient's anatomy before the real procedure. Tremor stabilisation filters out small hand shakes during microsurgery. Remote telesurgery uses networks and robotic arms to let a surgeon operate on a patient in another room or another city.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is real but uneven. Resection planning is furthest along, with AI models helping to mark margins on scans, though the final call still belongs to a surgeon. Haptic feedback is improving but still limited, because reproducing the feel of tissue through a machine is hard and often lags. Virtual rehearsal works for anatomy and approach, but it cannot predict how living tissue will bleed or move. Tremor stabilisation is reliable for small, high-frequency shakes, but it does not help with larger, slower movements. Remote telesurgery has been demonstrated, but it depends on fast, stable networks and is not routine. The honest limit is that these tools assist a surgeon, they do not replace judgment or handle unexpected complications.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages under this section move from planning to touch to practice to precision to distance. Resection Planning and Margins is the starting point, because it covers how AI helps define what to remove before any cut is made. Haptic Feedback in Robotic Surgery then explains what a surgeon feels through the instruments during the operation. Virtual Surgical Rehearsal sits between planning and the real procedure, letting a team test the steps on a digital copy of the patient. Tremor Stabilisation in Microsurgery addresses the fine motor control needed once the surgeon is working at very small scales. Remote Telesurgery is the last page, covering what happens when the surgeon is not in the same room as the patient. A reader would go to each page for a specific question, from margin decisions to the feel of tissue to the limits of operating over a network.
